extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating common ownership and applying 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections (and related 102(e)/(f)/(g) considerations), including required evidence, examiner procedures, form paragraphs, and special rules for biotechnology/process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership must exist at time the later invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ownership at the time the later invention was made is required to obviate a 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103, 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/103 or 35 U.S.C. 102(g)/103 rejection; a statement of present common ownership is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention is “made” when conception is complete (citing Mergenthaler v. Scudder and In re Tansel). Pfaff v. Wells guidance: the invention must be ready for patenting — e.g., drawings or descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention prior to the critical date. Common ownership at the time the later invention was made may be established irrespective of where the invention was made (U.S. or abroad), though 35 U.S.C. 104 continues to apply for other PTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable evidence to establish common ownership (37 CFR 1.104(a)(5) alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copending applications will be considered owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person if one of several showings is made: recorded assignments in the PTO; copies of unrecorded assignments filed in each application; an affidavit/declaration by the common owner averring common ownership and facts explaining why; or other evidence establishing common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments recorded in accordance with 37 CFR Part 3 that convey the entire rights to the same person are sufficient. Unrecorded assignment copies filed in each application are sufficient only if they convey the entire rights and — to establish ownership at the time the later invention was made — must contain language or be supplemented with evidence indicating relevant dates. Absent date-establishing language, additional evidence (e.g., an affidavit declaring inventors were under obligation to assign at the relevant time, employment agreements, or oaths/declarations) will be needed. Other evidence (e.g., a court decision) may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration requirements and who may sign for an organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations averring common ownership must be executed by the common owner or someone empowered to act on behalf of the corporation/organization; the requirements of 37 CFR 3.73(b) do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere power of attorney to prosecute an application does not make an individual an official of the corporation for purposes of averring common ownership. A patent attorney/agent or other individual may make such an affidavit only if a written appointment names them an official specifically empowered to make affidavits/declarations on behalf of the organization; the affidavit should refer to an attached copy of the written appointment and aver that the authority is still in effect. The original appointment need not be filed unless the PTO requires it. Corporations should give the written appointment only to persons who can know that common ownership exists and thus properly make affirmative representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should check assignment records (PALM) but not rely exclusively on them
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should check assignment records on the Patent Application Locating and Monitoring (PALM) system for patents and applications involved in rejections to determine possible common ownership or assignee relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment records on PALM show the execution date of any recorded assignment, but because applicants are not required to record assignments, PALM records are not the exclusive means for determining whether there was common ownership at the time the invention was made. Examiners should consider PALM records along with other evidence submitted in the file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific criteria to consider applications/patents as commonly owned at time of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and patents will be considered to be owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person, at the time the invention was made, if one of the following is shown: (A) PALM assignment records show common ownership/obligation at time of invention; (B) applicant provides evidence that the files refer to recorded assignments conveying entire rights at time of invention; (C) copies of unrecorded assignments conveying entire rights at time of invention are filed; (D) an affidavit/declaration by the common owner states there was common ownership at the time of invention and explains why; or (E) other evidence (e.g., court decision) establishes common ownership at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) and (l)(3) for additional information; applicants should provide date-revealing language when relying on assignment agreements to prove ownership at the relevant time, or supply supporting affidavits/documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure if common ownership is NOT established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the file does not establish common ownership at the time the invention was made, the examiner will assume the applications/patents are not commonly owned and will proceed with specified examination steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When common ownership is not established the examiner will: (A) assume not commonly owned; (B) examine the application on all grounds other than any conflict between the reference patent(s)/application(s) arising from a possible 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and/or (g); (C) consider applicability of any references under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and/or (g), including provisional rejections under 102(e)/103; and (D) apply the best references against the claimed invention by rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (including 103 based on 102(e),(f),(g)), until a statement establishing common ownership at the time of invention is made by the applicant. For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, examiners should anticipate that an affidavit averring common ownership may disqualify a patent/application cited under 102(e)/103; if such affidavit is filed in reply and claims are not amended, the examiner may not make the next Office action final if a new rejection is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership HAS been established (applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the file establishes that the application and any reference patent/application were owned by, or subject to an obligation/assignment to, the same person at the time the invention was made, the examiner should follow particular examination actions for applications filed on or after Nov 29, 1999.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner will: (A) examine the applications as to all grounds except 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and (g) as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103 (including provisional 102(e)/103 rejections); (B) examine for double patenting (statutory and nonstatutory) and make a provisional rejection if appropriate; and (C) invite the applicant to file a terminal disclaimer to overcome any provisional or actual nonstatutory double patenting rejection, if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership HAS been established (applications filed prior to Nov 29, 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed prior to Nov 29, 1999, even if the application and reference were commonly owned at the time the later invention was made, different rules apply concerning prior art status under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner will: (A) examine as to all grounds except 35 U.S.C. 102(f) and (g) as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103; (B) examine for double patenting and make a provisional rejection if appropriate; (C) examine the later filed application under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as it applies through 35 U.S.C. 103 and make a provisional 102(e)/103 rejection in the later filed application, if appropriate; and (D) invite the applicant to file a terminal disclaimer to overcome provisional/actual nonstatutory double patenting and permit the applicant to file affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131, or a terminal disclaimer with an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130, or an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the invention is not “by another,” to overcome the provisional or actual 102(e)/103 rejection, if appropriate. Note: An affidavit under 37 CFR 1.130 cannot be used to overcome a provisional 102(e)/103 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting rejections and how to overcome them
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting, including statutory and nonstatutory double patenting, even if the later-filed application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections prevent an organization from obtaining multiple patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. They can be overcome in certain circumstances by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321, the terminal portion of the term of the later patent and including in the disclaimer a provision that the patent is enforceable only while commonly owned with the application/patent forming the basis for the rejection, thereby eliminating extension of patent life. See MPEP § 804 and § 804.02 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraph 7.20 (Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 103(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.20 quotes 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and serves as the statutory basis for obviousness rejections in Office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) The statute need not be cited in all Office actions; it is only required in first actions on the merits employing 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and in final rejections. (2) This paragraph should be used only once in a given Office action. (3) This paragraph must precede paragraphs 7.20.01 - 7.22 when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs addressing art disqualified by common ownership (7.20.01, 7.20.03) and joint inventors presumption (7.20.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific form paragraphs instruct examiners on language to use when applied art is disqualified due to common ownership and on presuming common ownership among joint inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶7.20.01: For applications filed prior to Nov 29, 1999 — indicates the applied art is disqualified under 102(f)/(g) but may still qualify under another subsection of 102; advises how applicant may overcome (37 CFR 1.132 or 1.131). ¶7.20.03: For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999 — analogous wording for 102(e),(f),(g). ¶7.20.02: Joint inventors — presumes subject matter of various claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were made absent evidence to the contrary; instructs applicant of obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to identify inventor and invention dates for claims not commonly owned to allow examiner to consider 103(c) and potential prior art under 102(e),(f),(g). Use notes specify mandatory usage conditions (e.g., must be used in all applications with joint inventors unless claims restricted to one invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejection form paragraph 7.21.01 (copending application with common assignee or common inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶7.21.01 is used to provisionally reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over a copending application that has a common assignee or at least one common inventor, based on the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provisional rejection may be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that disclosure in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the instant application (not an invention “by another”); (2) showing an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131; or (for applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999) showing that the subject matter of reference and claimed invention were owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made. Examiner Notes explain proper use cases, limitations, and cross-references (e.g., use paragraph 7.15.01 if claimed invention is fully disclosed in copending application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.21 and 7.21.02 — rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) with common assignee/inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶7.21 used for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) with explanation applying Graham v. Deere test; ¶7.21.02 is used when the applied reference has a common assignee or at least one common inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶7.21 must be preceded by 7.20 or 7.103 and followed by full explanation applying Graham. ¶7.21.02 includes ways the rejection might be overcome: (1) 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation; (2) 37 CFR 1.131 showing earlier date of invention; or (3) 37 CFR 1.130 affidavit + terminal disclaimer (for certain circumstances). Notes spell out appropriate usage and exceptions (e.g., not to be used in certain post-Nov 29, 1999 situations where common ownership is established in the file).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere Test for Obviousness (¶7.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries from Graham v. John Deere Co. applied to establish background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) determine scope and contents of prior art; (2) ascertain differences between prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolve level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) consider objective evidence (secondary considerations) present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph may be used, if appropriate, in response to an argument invoking Graham v. Deere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection usage and examples (¶7.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶7.27 permits a combined rejection — claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 as anticipated or, alternatively, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious — when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended as a common substitute for distinct 102 or 103 rejections; examiners should make a single appropriate rejection when possible. Examples of when to use ¶7.27 include: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation supports 102 and another supports 103; (b) when a reference discloses all limitations except a property/function and the examiner cannot determine inherent possession vs obvious variant (In re Fitzgerald); (c) genus/species issues (In re Schaumann); (d) product-by-process claims produced by different processes (In re Marosi, In re Thorpe); (e) means-plus-function uncertainty; (f) overlapping ranges with no specific example in reference. When used, include a full explanation and precede with required paragraphs (e.g., 7.07 and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnological process treatment under 35 U.S.C. 103(b) (706.02(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) provides a special rule for certain biotechnological processes: a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel and nonobvious shall be considered nonobvious if specific conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements of 103(b): (A) process and composition claims are in same application or in separate applications having same effective filing date; (B) both process and composition were owned or subject to assignment to same person at the time the process was invented; (C) a patent on the process must also contain composition claims or, if composition is in another patent, the patents must expire same date; (D) the process must fall within 103(b)'s definition of biotechnological process (e.g., genetic alteration to express exogenous nucleotide sequence, cell fusion yielding cell line expressing a protein, methods using products produced by such processes); and (E) a timely election to proceed under 103(b) must be made via petition under 37 CFR 1.182. Election timeliness: normally no later than earlier of payment of issue fee or filing of appeal brief where composition claim not rejected; special transitional rules for certain pending applications described. Generally, reliance on 103(b) should be rare in view of Federal Circuit decisions (In re Ochiai; In re Brouwer). See 35 U.S.C. 282 for effect on presumption of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of prior art rejections over non-prior-art ('technical') rejections (706.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether claims are patentable over the prior art; undue emphasis on non-prior-art or technical rejections should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner effort should concentrate on truly essential matters; minimize effort on technical rejections that are not critical. Where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., insufficient disclosure, undue breadth, utility issues), the rejection should be fully developed with reasons rather than terse conclusions or stereotyped expressions.
